levels.name: Ben, 24, Night-Shift Janitor
levels.story: The 8 levels of hitting snooze 7 times. Level 1. Level 1: 7 snoozes pressed, and my forehead badge is flashing red like a crime scene. My tiny studio apartment smells of stale instant ramen and pure desperation. The digital clock on the wall glows 7:42 AM, and my shift started twelve minutes ago across town. I smash the snooze button for the seventh time, watching the tiny gold coin roll under my battered sneaker. "Still in bed while the real workers are making money? You'll never afford rent in this city with numbers like that!" I pull the heavy weighted blanket over my head, my phone vibrating furiously with missed calls from my boss. Then he said this one sentence that completely shattered my remaining dignity. You'll see that in Level 2.

levels.name: Chloe, 26, Barista
levels.story: The 8 levels of hitting snooze 7 times. Level 2. Level 2: Five snoozes deep and my espresso machine is hissing louder than my boss's complaints. My forehead glows a faint orange as I pour oat milk into a cardboard cup at 7:55 AM. The cafe smells like burned roast beans and Monday morning panic. "You look like you slept in a dumpster, sweetheart. Hurry up with my macchiato!" I force a fake smile while hiding a tiny gold coin beneath the tip jar. Suddenly, the train schedule board outside flickers violently, and my phone buzzes with a shocking text message from my roommate. Then he said this one sentence that completely changed the morning rush. You'll see that in Level 3.

levels.name: Marcus, 31, Junior Analyst
levels.story: The 8 levels of hitting snooze 7 times. Level 3. Level 3: Four snoozes and my tie is knotted so tight I can barely breathe in this elevator. My forehead badge shines a steady yellow as the brass doors slide open on the 14th floor of the financial tower. The office smells like expensive cologne and pure corporate anxiety at 8:15 AM. My hands tremble as I open my laptop to find my quarterly metrics completely blank. Then she said this one sentence that made my stomach drop straight to the floor. You'll see that in Level 4.

levels.name: Elena, 29, Graphic Designer
levels.story: The 8 levels of hitting snooze 7 times. Level 4. Level 4: Three snoozes and my graphic tablet stylus is practically burning a hole in my pocket. My forehead badge glows a soft green as I rush through the revolving doors of the creative agency at 8:30 AM. The studio smells like fresh printer toner and expensive artisanal matcha tea. "Your vector mockups were due ten minutes ago, Elena. We're pitching to the clients right now!" I quickly close three open browser tabs while kicking a tiny gold coin under the heavy drafting table. My screen flickers, and my design files vanish into a corrupted folder. Then he said this one sentence that completely wrecked my creative flow. You'll see that in Level 5.

levels.name: David, 35, Senior Architect
levels.story: The 8 levels of hitting snooze 7 times. Level 5. Level 5: Two snoozes and my blueprints are rolled tighter than my nerves at 8:45 AM. My forehead badge shines a bright blue as I step out onto the steel balcony of the high-rise construction site. The morning air smells like damp concrete, welding sparks, and cold black coffee. "Your structural calculations for the North Wing are off by two inches, David! Fix it before the inspector arrives." I swallow hard, sliding a tiny gold coin beneath a heavy stack of architectural blueprints. My phone lights up with an urgent email from the city planning commission. Then he said this one sentence that made me question my entire career. You'll see that in Level 6.

levels.name: Celeste, 45, Founder & CEO
levels.story: The 8 levels of hitting snooze 7 times. Level 8. Level 8: Seven snoozes pressed, and I was the one who programmed every single alarm in this city. My forehead badge glows with an infinite gold symbol as I stand on the private roof terrace overlooking the entire skyline at 9:30 AM. The air smells like fresh morning rain and absolute victory. Ben, the tired janitor from Level 1, looks up from the rainy alley below as his phone finally stops ringing. "The number on your forehead never lies," I whisper, holding the master control remote that links every single snooze button in the metropolis. I toss a tiny gold coin over the glass railing, watching it spin down through the clouds. The entire city digital display flickers and resets to zero in perfect synchronization. What happens when the person at the very top decides to hit snooze just one last time?
